routing_warnings.description: The client conditionally requests delivery of the created template for future in-house production; this concerns source-file handoff rather than template creation.
The client directly requests that the existing template be sent, which is a handoff obligation rather than a change to template creation.
The client reiterates that the template must be delivered before the project concludes.
The freelancer claims that the template and other project files have been delivered through a shared folder.
The requested reduction of the author element concerns author presentation; the general approval of the draft direction does not verify the completed issue assembly.

The empty areas at article endings are a concrete failure of the narrower article-ending balance Requirement; the message also contains separate clauses for advertisement quality, typography, cover references, spread compatibility, and contents accuracy.
Changing the issue from November to December affects the issue date and edition label rather than the magazine assembly mechanism.
The remaining large white areas and requested subject-related images concern the independently testable article-ending balance Requirement.
Restricting additional images to pages with huge empty spaces modifies the narrower article-ending balance behavior.
The request to reduce the oversized author element concerns author presentation rather than the issue-wide visual-style Requirement.
The restriction on red in the Dorian Vale article belongs to the dedicated article-color Requirement.
The request for a thicker, easier-to-read article font concerns the independent body-typography Requirement.
The approval concerns a specific image-edge treatment rather than the issue-wide visual direction.
This message requires inclusion and placement of three specific cover-mentioned articles; their website URLs identify the content but do not change the established website-sourcing rule.
The requested reduction concerns the visual size of the author element rather than author identity or photo correctness.
The request to replace the incorrect author photograph concerns author identity and photo selection rather than the portrait's shape or size.
The message specifically reports an image-edge fading and page-blending treatment, not completion of balanced article endings as a whole.
The client approves the specific image-edge treatment described in message 163; this does not verify all article-ending balance behavior.
The final review broadly verifies the cohesive issue layout, page structure, and article flow without specifically confirming that all article-ending white-space issues were resolved.
This message claims implementation of contents-to-chapter and return navigation links, not accuracy of the table-of-contents listings or page numbers.
The request to test the flip book concerns its operational spread compatibility rather than production of the PDF artifact itself.
The source removes the need for a print version; its launch-time language is project scheduling rather than a change to the digital PDF artifact.
The client's decision to perform the Heyzine upload through a white-label account changes the platform and upload workflow rather than the PDF deliverable.
The preview-only restriction concerns which file may be uploaded to Heyzine, not production of the final digital PDF generally.
The instruction to upload the supplied copy on Heyzine identifies the designated upload file rather than changing the platform or white-label workflow.
The review verifies that delivered files were prepared for digital flipbook distribution but does not verify white-label branding or completion of the client-managed Heyzine upload.
The separate clause about manually repairing flattened 72-ppi advertisements belongs to the advertisement-rendering Requirement.
The request to add subject-related images to large empty page areas concerns article-ending layout balance, not technical image-quality correction.
Fading an inserted image into the white page is a placement and layout treatment rather than correction of low-resolution imagery.
The client's approval verifies the image-edge layout treatment described in message 163, not the publication image-quality Requirement.
